vtrmc-1989-01.title: Similar triangles and AM-GM
vtrmc-1989-01.body:
The top side of the square is a segment of length $a$ parallel to the base, at height $a$. It cuts off a small triangle at the top, similar to the whole triangle, with base $a$ and height $h-a$. By similarity
$$\frac ab=\frac{h-a}{h}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad ah=bh-ab\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=\frac{bh}{b+h}.$$
Hence
$$\frac{a^2}{\tfrac12bh}=\frac{2bh}{(b+h)^2}\le\frac{2bh}{4bh}=\frac12,$$
using $(b+h)^2-4bh=(b-h)^2\ge0$. So the area of the square is at most half the area of the triangle, with equality iff $b=h$. ∎

vtrmc-1989-01.title: Harmonic mean
vtrmc-1989-01.body:
From $a=\frac{bh}{b+h}$ (similar triangles, as in the first approach) we get
$$\frac1a=\frac1b+\frac1h .$$
By AM-GM, $\frac1b+\frac1h\ge\frac{2}{\sqrt{bh}}$, so $a\le\frac{\sqrt{bh}}2$ and
$$a^2\le\frac{bh}{4}=\frac12\cdot\Big(\frac12bh\Big).$$
∎

vtrmc-1989-02.title: Expand along rows
vtrmc-1989-02.body:
Every $2\times2$ matrix with entries in $\{0,1\}$ has determinant $ps-qr\in\{-1,0,1\}$, since $ps,qr\in\{0,1\}$.

Expanding along the first row,
$$\det A=a_{11}M_{11}-a_{12}M_{12}+a_{13}M_{13},$$
a sum of three terms, each a product of an entry in $\{0,1\}$ and a minor in $\{-1,0,1\}$. So $|\det A|\le3$.

**(a)** If $\det A=\pm3$, all three terms must be $\pm1$ with the same sign, so in particular $a_{11}=a_{12}=a_{13}=1$. Expanding along the second row in the same way shows $a_{21}=a_{22}=a_{23}=1$. Then the first two rows are equal and $\det A=0$, a contradiction. So $\det A\ne\pm3$.

**(b)** By the above, $\det A\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. All these values occur:
- $0$: the zero matrix; $1$: the identity; $-1$: the identity with two rows swapped;
- $2$: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\det A=1\cdot(1-0)-0+1\cdot(1-0)=2$;
- $-2$: the same matrix with its first two columns interchanged.

**Answer: $\det A\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$.** ∎

vtrmc-1989-02.title: Counting the permutation terms
vtrmc-1989-02.body:
By the Leibniz formula $\det A=\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)a_{1\sigma(1)}a_{2\sigma(2)}a_{3\sigma(3)}$: three even permutations contribute $0$ or $+1$ each, three odd ones $0$ or $-1$ each. So $\det A=P-N$ with $P,N\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the numbers of nonzero even and odd terms.

$\det A=3$ needs $P=3$: the three even permutations are the identity and the two $3$-cycles, whose "positions" together cover all $9$ entries, so $A$ is all ones, and then $N=3$ as well — $\det A=0$. Similarly $\det A=-3$ forces all ones. So $|\det A|\le2$, and the examples in the first approach show that each value $-2,-1,0,1,2$ occurs. (A computer check of all $2^9=512$ matrices confirms the set $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$.) ∎

vtrmc-1989-03.title: Find the coefficients
vtrmc-1989-03.body:
To find the combination, solve $\lambda(1,0,1)+\mu(0,-1,1)=(2,-1,3)$: the first coordinate gives $\lambda=2$, the second $\mu=1$, and the third checks: $2+1=3$. Then $\mathbf x=\lambda(-1,3,2)+\mu(2,-2,1)=(-2+2,\,6-2,\,4+1)=(0,4,5)$.

(The solution need not be unique if $A$ is singular, but $(0,4,5)$ is always a solution.)

**Answer: $(0,4,5)$.**

vtrmc-1989-04.title: Factor $9$ into distinct integers
vtrmc-1989-04.body:
We have $(r-a)(r-b)(r-c)(r-d)=9$ and the four factors are distinct integers (as $a,b,c,d$ are distinct). Each factor divides $9$, so lies in $\{\pm1,\pm3,\pm9\}$.

If some factor were $\pm9$, the other three would have product $\pm1$, so each would be $\pm1$ — but there are only two distinct values $\pm1$ available for three distinct factors. So all factors lie in $\{\pm1,\pm3\}$, and being four distinct numbers they are exactly $1,-1,3,-3$ (whose product is indeed $9$). Therefore
$$(r-a)+(r-b)+(r-c)+(r-d)=1-1+3-3=0,$$
i.e. $4r=a+b+c+d$. ∎

vtrmc-1989-04.title: Absolute values
vtrmc-1989-04.body: Let $u_1,\dots,u_4$ be the distinct integers $r-a,\dots,r-d$, with $|u_1u_2u_3u_4|=9$. At most two of them have absolute value $1$ (namely $1$ and $-1$), so at least two have absolute value $\ge2$, hence $\ge3$ (they divide $9$). Then $|u_iu_j|\ge9$ for those two, forcing the other two to have absolute value $1$ and the big two to have absolute value exactly $3$. Distinctness gives $\{u_i\}=\{1,-1,3,-3\}$, whose sum is $0$, so $4r-(a+b+c+d)=0$. ∎

**(ii)** Note that

e0$. Also $f_n(0)=1$. So $f_n$ has no real zero, and by continuity and $f_n(0)=1>0$, $f_n>0$ on $\mathbb R$, completing the induction. ∎

vtrmc-1989-05.title: Direct bound for (i)
vtrmc-1989-05.body:
**(i)** Alternatively, for $x\ge0$ all terms are $\ge0$ and the constant is $1$, so $f_0(x)\ge1$. For $x<0$ write
$$f_0(x)=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1=x^2\Big(x+\frac12\Big)^2+\frac34x^2+x+1=x^2\Big(x+\frac12\Big)^2+\frac34\Big(x+\frac23\Big)^2+\frac23>0 .$$
(Check: $x^2(x^2+x+\frac14)+\frac34x^2+x+1=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1$, and $\frac34(x+\frac23)^2+\frac23=\frac34x^2+x+\frac13+\frac23$.) So $f_0>0$ everywhere.

**(ii)** then follows by the same induction as in the first approach. ∎

vtrmc-1989-06.title: $g$ is an involution
vtrmc-1989-06.body:
For $x>1$, $g(x)=\frac{x}{x-1}>1$ and
$$g(g(x))=\frac{\frac{x}{x-1}}{\frac{x}{x-1}-1}=\frac{x}{x-(x-1)}=x .$$
Hence $f^k(x)=x$ for even $k$ and $f^k(x)=\frac{x}{x-1}$ for odd $k$. Splitting the (absolutely convergent) series,
$$\sum_{k=0}^\infty2^{-k}f^k(x)=x\Big(1+\frac14+\frac1{16}+\cdots\Big)+\frac{x}{x-1}\Big(\frac12+\frac18+\cdots\Big)=\frac43x+\frac23\cdot\frac{x}{x-1}.$$
Combining,
$$\frac{4x(x-1)+2x}{3(x-1)}=\frac{4x^2-2x}{3x-3}.$$
**Answer: $\dfrac{4x^2-2x}{3x-3}$** (so $a=4$, $b=-2$, $c=0$, $d=3$, $e=-3$, up to a common factor).

vtrmc-1989-06.title: Functional equation for the sum
vtrmc-1989-06.body:
Let $S(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}f^k(x)$ (convergent since the terms take only two values). Since $f^{k}(x)=f^{k-1}(g(x))$,
$$S(x)=x+\frac12S(g(x)),\qquad S(g(x))=g(x)+\frac12S(x)$$
(using $g(g(x))=x$). Substituting the second into the first: $S=x+\frac12g+\frac14S$, so
$$S(x)=\frac43\Big(x+\frac{x}{2(x-1)}\Big)=\frac{4x(x-1)+2x}{3(x-1)}=\frac{4x^2-2x}{3x-3}.$$
Numerically, at $x=2.5$ both the series and the formula give $4.444\ldots$

**Answer: $\dfrac{4x^2-2x}{3x-3}$.**

vtrmc-1989-07.title: Eliminate the prices
vtrmc-1989-07.body:
Let the price be $x$ dollars before noon and $y$ after noon, $x>y>0$, and let the farmers sell $p,q,s$ chickens before noon ($1\le p\le9$, $1\le q\le15$, $1\le s\le25$). Then
$$px+(10-p)y=35,\qquad qx+(16-q)y=35,\qquad sx+(26-s)y=35 .$$
With $d=x-y>0$ these read
$$pd+10y=35,\qquad qd+16y=35,\qquad sd+26y=35 .$$
Subtracting consecutive equations: $(p-q)d=6y$ and $(q-s)d=10y$. Both right sides are positive, so $p>q>s$ and
$$\frac{p-q}{q-s}=\frac35 .$$
Thus $p-q=3k$, $q-s=5k$ for a positive integer $k$, and $p=s+8k\le9$ with $s\ge1$ forces $k=1$, $s=1$, $p=9$, $q=6$.

Then $3d=6y$, so $d=2y$, and $9\cdot2y+10y=28y=35$, giving $y=\frac54$ and $x=y+d=\frac{15}4$.

Check: $9(3.75)+1(1.25)=35$, $6(3.75)+10(1.25)=35$, $1(3.75)+25(1.25)=35$. ✓

**Answer: \$3.75 per chicken before noon and \$1.25 after noon.**

(The official solution sheet's determinant method is the same idea; its stated values $b=8$, $c=9$ are misprints for $6$ and $1$ — they do not satisfy the equations.)

vtrmc-1989-07.title: Exhaustive check
vtrmc-1989-07.body:
For each choice of $(p,q)$ with $1\le p\le9$, $1\le q\le15$, solve the first two equations for $(x,y)$ and test the third equation for some $1\le s\le25$ together with $x>y>0$. A short computer search finds only $(p,q,s)=(9,6,1)$ with $(x,y)=(3.75,1.25)$, confirming uniqueness.

By hand one can also see the structure: the farmer with the most chickens must sell the fewest before noon (his many cheap afternoon sales compensate), and the totals $35=9\cdot\frac{15}4+\frac54$, $35=6\cdot\frac{15}4+10\cdot\frac54$, $35=\frac{15}4+25\cdot\frac54$ show every farmer earns the same.

**Answer: \$3.75 before noon, \$1.25 after noon.**

vtrmc-1989-08.title: Count zeros and nonzero terms
vtrmc-1989-08.body:
**Sum of the terms.** Each $a_j\le n$; if $a_j=n$ then every term equals $j$, so $a_j=j<n$, a contradiction. Hence all terms lie in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, and counting the $n$ terms by their values gives
$$a_0+a_1+\dots+a_{n-1}=n .$$

**$a_0\ge1$.** If $a_0=0$, no term is $0$, so all $a_i\ge1$; with sum $n$, all $a_i=1$, but then $a_1=n\ne1$. So $m:=a_0\ge1$.

**Structure of $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$.** The $m$ zero terms are among $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ (as $a_0\ne0$), so exactly $n-1-m$ of $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ are nonzero, and they sum to $n-m=(n-1-m)+1$. Positive integers summing to one more than their number: exactly one of them is $2$ and the rest are $1$. So $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ consist of one $2$, $n-2-m$ ones and $m$ zeros.

**Cases.**
- $m=1$: the ones in the sequence are $a_0$ and $n-2-m$ others, so $a_1=n-2$; but $a_1\le2$, so $n\le4$.
- $m=2$: $a_1=n-2-m=n-4\le2$, so $n\le6$.
- $m\ge3$: the value $m$ occurs (as $a_0$) and no $a_i$ with $i\ge1$ exceeds $2$, so $a_m=1$. The value $2$ occurs exactly once (it is not $a_0$), so $a_2=1$. Which index $j\ge1$ carries the single $2$? $a_j=2$ means the value $j$ occurs twice. Values $\ge3$ occur only as $a_0$ (once); $a_2=1$, $a_m=1$; so $j=1$: $a_1=2$. Then the ones among $a_1,\dots$ are exactly $a_2$ and $a_m$, so $n-2-m=2$, i.e. $m=n-4$, and all other terms are $0$.

Hence for $n\ge7$ (where only $m\ge3$ is possible) the sequence must be
$$a_0=n-4,\quad a_1=2,\quad a_2=1,\quad a_{n-4}=1,\quad a_i=0\text{ otherwise}.$$
It works: there are $n-4$ zeros, two ones ($a_2,a_{n-4}$), one $2$ ($a_1$), one $n-4$ ($a_0$; note $n-4\ge3$), and no other values. So the sequence exists and is unique.

**(b)** For $n=7$: $\{3,2,1,1,0,0,0\}$. ∎

vtrmc-1989-08.title: Weighted sum
vtrmc-1989-08.body:
Besides $\sum_i a_i=n$ (see the first approach), the sum of all terms counted by value is $\sum_i i\,a_i$, so $\sum_i i\,a_i=n$ too. Subtracting,
$$\sum_{i\ge2}(i-1)a_i=a_0=:m\ge1 .\qquad(*)$$
Also $a_1=n-m-\sum_{i\ge2}a_i$.

- $m=1$: $(*)$ forces $a_2=1$ and $a_i=0$ for $i\ge3$, so $a_1=n-2\ge5$. But the only possible ones in the sequence are $a_0$, $a_2$ and $a_1$, so $a_1\le3$ — contradiction.
- $m=2$: $(*)$ gives either $a_2=2$ (others $i\ge3$ zero) or $a_3=1$ (others $i\ge2$ zero). In the first case $a_1=n-4\ge3$ but no term other than possibly $a_1$ equals $1$; in the second $a_1=n-3\ge4$ but the only ones are $a_3$ and possibly $a_1$. Contradiction.
- $m\ge3$: the value $m$ occurs, so $a_m\ge1$; since $2(m-1)>m$, $(*)$ gives $a_m=1$, and the remaining contribution $1$ forces $a_2=1$, all other $a_i=0$ ($i\ge3$, $i\ne m$). Then $a_1=n-m-2$. The ones are $a_2$, $a_m$, and $a_1$ if $a_1=1$; so $a_1=2$ (the values $0,1,\ge3$ all lead to a contradiction), whence $m=n-4$.

So for $n\ge7$ the sequence is $(n-4,2,1,0,\dots,0,1,0,0,0)$ with the second $1$ at position $n-4$; for $n=7$ it is $3,2,1,1,0,0,0$. A computer search over all candidates for $n\le12$ confirms this (and finds none for $n=6$). ∎
